title: Tell me about a time you improved the performance of a slow system — what was slow, what did you change, and what was the improvement?
shortTitle: Tell me about a time you improved the performance of a slow system — what was slow, what you changed, and the improvement
topicTitle: Tell me about a time you improved the performance of a slow system

s1_definition.profdef: This question tests your performance-engineering discipline. The interviewer wants to see that you measured before changing, found the real bottleneck with profiling or metrics, made a targeted fix, and verified the improvement with before-and-after numbers. A strong answer leads with data and resists the temptation to guess at optimizations.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This question tests your performance-engineering discipline. The interviewer wants to see that you measured before changing, found the real bottleneck with profiling or metrics, made a targeted fix, and verified the improvement with before-and-after numbers. A strong answer leads with data and resists the temptation to guess at optimizations.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine customers complaining that the bank's loan-approval desk is slow. A guesser hires more staff randomly. A professional first measures where the time goes — forms take two minutes, but the credit check takes twenty — then fixes the credit check specifically. The improvement is measured: approvals go from twenty-five minutes to seven. That measure-first, fix-the-bottleneck discipline is exactly what this question rewards.

**One line to remember:** Measure first, fix the real bottleneck, verify with before-and-after numbers — never optimize on a guess.

sections.s2_technical:
The STAR structure anchors this. Situation — what was slow and how you knew (user complaints, SLA breaches, a slow endpoint). Task — your ownership of the fix. Action — the measurement, the bottleneck you found, and the targeted change. Result — the quantified improvement. The non-negotiable senior behavior is measuring before and after, because performance intuition is famously unreliable.

Start by quantifying the slowness with a real metric, not a vibe. "The account-statement endpoint had a p99 latency of three seconds, breaching our one-second SLA." Then you profile to find the bottleneck. In a banking backend the usual suspects are database queries (N+1 query patterns, missing indexes), unnecessary serialization, lock contention, or synchronous calls that should be parallel. The classic N+1 problem looks like loading a list and then querying inside a loop: `for (Account a : accounts) { txns.add(txnRepo.findByAccount(a.getId())); }` fires one query per account. The fix is a single batched query, `txnRepo.findByAccountIdIn(ids)`, turning N+1 queries into one.

The change must be targeted at the measured bottleneck, not a scattershot of micro-optimizations. If the profile shows ninety percent of time in one query, you fix that query — perhaps adding an index, so a full table scan becomes an index seek. You can express the measured win precisely: `log.info(() -> "p99 before=" + before + "ms after=" + after + "ms")`. Caching is another common lever: if balance lookups dominate and tolerate slight staleness, a short-TTL cache turns a database hit into a memory read, but you apply it only where correctness allows.

A senior nuance is to verify the fix did not break correctness — a faster wrong answer is worse than a slow right one, especially with money. Another nuance is to measure under realistic load, because a change that helps a single request can hurt under concurrency, and vice versa. A further nuance is to state the improvement as a business-relevant number — latency, throughput, or cost — and to mention any trade-off you accepted, such as slightly stale cached data, so the answer is honest about costs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The account-statement screen is painfully slow. The real banking problem is that to show a customer's statement, the code loads the account and then, for each of its transactions, makes a separate database call to fetch details — the classic N+1 query pattern. This is exactly like a teller who walks to the archive once per transaction instead of fetching them all in one trip.

Problem 2 — A developer tries to "optimize" by tweaking unrelated code without measuring, and nothing improves. This is like hiring more tellers when the real delay is the archive trips. The fix is to measure, find the N+1 bottleneck, and batch the queries into one.

To make this runnable, we will simulate the slow statement generation and its fix. A `StatementService` can generate a statement in two ways: a slow way that simulates one query per transaction (N+1), and a fast way that simulates a single batched query. A `PerformanceHarness` times both and reports the before-and-after with a speedup factor. The `PerfDemo` main class runs the harness so the reader sees measurement first, the targeted change from N+1 to batched, and the verified improvement as real timing numbers.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's account SAV2001 with a statement of five hundred transactions. Each simulated database round-trip costs about one millisecond.

Step 1: The harness measures the slow path first. The slow method makes one query for the account, then one query for each of the five hundred transactions, totaling five hundred and one round-trips, roughly five hundred and one milliseconds.

Step 2: The harness logs the slow timing as a warning, because a p99 in this range would breach a one-second SLA under real conditions.

Step 3: The harness measures the fast path. The fast method makes one query for the account plus one batched query for all transactions, totaling just two round-trips, roughly two milliseconds.

Step 4: The harness logs the fast timing. The same data is produced; only the number of database round-trips changed, from N plus one down to two. This is the targeted fix to the measured bottleneck.

Step 5: The harness computes the speedup by dividing the slow time by the fast time, yielding a large factor, and logs the verified improvement as a before-and-after. The improvement is a derived measurement, not an assumption.

```
WARNING: SLOW (N+1): 503ms for 500 txns
INFO: FAST (batched): 2ms for 500 txns
INFO: IMPROVEMENT: ~251x faster (503ms to 2ms)
```

```
  Slow account-statement screen (500 txns)
    │
    ▼
  PerformanceHarness.compare()
    │ MEASURE slow:  1 + N queries  → ~503ms  (N+1 bottleneck)
    │ CHANGE:        batch into 1 query for all txns
    │ MEASURE fast:  1 + 1 queries  → ~2ms
    ▼
  VERIFY: ~251x faster (503ms → 2ms), same data
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The slow system I improved was our account-statement screen. Customers were complaining that pulling up a statement took around three seconds, which breached our one-second latency target, and it was worst for customers with long transaction histories. I owned the fix. The first thing I did — and this is the part I think matters most — was measure rather than guess. I profiled the endpoint and the data was unambiguous: almost all the time was spent in the database, not in the application logic.

When I looked closer, it was a classic N plus one query problem. To build the statement, the code loaded the account and then fired a separate database query for every single transaction. For a customer with five hundred transactions, that was over five hundred round-trips to the database, and each round-trip has a cost that adds up quickly. The fix was targeted at exactly that bottleneck: instead of querying per transaction, I batched them into a single query that fetched all the transactions at once. Same data, same correctness, but two round-trips instead of five hundred and one.

The improvement was dramatic and, importantly, measured. In my test the slow path took around half a second for five hundred transactions and the batched version took a couple of milliseconds — well over a hundred times faster — and in production the p99 for that endpoint dropped comfortably under our SLA. I verified the output was identical before and after, because a faster but wrong statement would be far worse than a slow correct one, especially with money.

The reason I tell it this way is that performance work lives or dies on discipline. I always measure before I change anything, because intuition about performance is unreliable and it is easy to waste days optimizing code that was never the bottleneck. I fix the specific thing the profiler points to rather than scattering micro-optimizations, I verify with real before-and-after numbers under realistic load, and I am honest about any trade-off. Here there was no correctness trade-off — just far fewer database calls — which is the cleanest kind of win.
